set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Which household exposure is a known source of Salmonella?
opts: Keeping live backyard hens

Correct. Live poultry such as backyard hens is a Salmonella source alongside poultry products, eggs and pet food, which fits its association mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles. Raw honey and garden soil, by contrast, are where clostridial spores are found.
Moldy bread left in the pantry
Mold on bread is fungal spoilage, and fungi do not commonly cause disease; moldy bread is not a Salmonella source. Live backyard poultry is, along with poultry products, eggs and pet food.
Digging in garden soil

Soil holds clostridial spores, and Listeria monocytogenes can persist in it; garden soil is not a Salmonella exposure here. Keeping live backyard hens is, since Salmonella is associated mainly with poultry.
Raw honey kept in the pantry

Raw honey is where spores of clostridia can be found, a Clostridium concern rather than a Salmonella one. The household Salmonella exposure is live poultry such as backyard hens, matching its main poultry reservoir.

mis.Moldy bread left in the pantry: spoilage fungi confused with a pathogen source

set1.io: 4 — Correlate associations between improved laboratory analytical methods with respect to near-daily announcements of food recalls and food-related illness
set1.q: A laboratory wants to confirm Escherichia coli in a water sample, not link it to other isolates. Which tool is often used?
opts: A PulseNet database search

PulseNet is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention database of isolate patterns, used to find outbreak causes. Confirming Escherichia coli in a water sample is done on eosin methylene blue plates.
A federal food recall search

Federal websites such as the Food and Drug Administration and United States Department of Agriculture sites list recalled foods. Confirming Escherichia coli in a water sample is a laboratory task done on eosin methylene blue plates.
Eosin methylene blue plates

Correct. Eosin methylene blue plates are often used to confirm Escherichia coli in samples such as food and water. Escherichia coli is an indicator organism associated with human and animal feces, so confirming it points to fecal contamination.
Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis

Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis makes a band pattern for each isolate so that isolates can be compared and outbreaks traced. The task here is confirming Escherichia coli in a sample, which eosin methylene blue plates do.

mis.A PulseNet database search: database confused with a laboratory test
mis.A federal food recall search: recall listings confused with a laboratory test

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: How do recorded counts of foodborne illness compare with the true number of cases?
opts: Low for viruses, accurate for bacteria

Under-reporting is not limited to viruses: Campylobacter jejuni, a bacterium, is very much under-reported, and the overall foodborne count, in which bacteria are the most common pathogens, is probably under-reported as well.
They are probably too low

Correct. The yearly estimate of foodborne illness is described as probably an under-reported number, and Campylobacter jejuni illness in particular is very much under-reported. Many people who fall ill are never counted, so recorded counts likely understate the true burden.
They are probably too high

The direction is reversed. Foodborne illness numbers are described as probably under-reported, meaning real cases outnumber recorded ones; Campylobacter jejuni illness is singled out as very much under-reported.
They match closely, thanks to surveillance

Surveillance by health departments and federal agencies helps, and tracking reduces detection time and the number of cases, but the counts are still described as probably under-reported. The true number of cases is likely higher than the record.

mis.They match closely, thanks to surveillan: surveillance assumed to capture every case
mis.Low for viruses, accurate for bacteria: bacterial illness assumed to be fully counted

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: When is a person with hepatitis A most contagious?
opts: At the height of the symptoms

Contagiousness peaks before illness is visible, about two weeks before symptoms appear, not at the worst of the symptoms. That is why handwashing and diaper hygiene matter even around people who seem well.
About two weeks after symptoms
This reverses the timing: a person with hepatitis A is most contagious about two weeks BEFORE symptoms appear, not after. The fecal-oral route spreads it during that earlier window.
About two weeks before symptoms

Correct. With the fecal-oral hepatitis viruses, a person is most contagious about two weeks before symptoms appear. That silent window is why handwashing, diaper hygiene, thorough cooking and clean drinking water matter, and a vaccine exists for suspected exposure.
On the very first day of symptoms
The most contagious time comes earlier, about two weeks before symptoms appear, so a person can spread hepatitis A before feeling ill. Waiting for symptoms misses that window.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Which kinds of Escherichia coli strains carry numerous toxins that make them harmful?
opts: Salt-tolerant strains from estuarine water

Salt tolerance in ocean and estuarine waters describes Vibrio species, not harmful Escherichia coli. The bad Escherichia coli strains carrying numerous toxins are enterotoxigenic and enterohemorrhagic strains.
Fermenting strains used in yogurt making

Yogurt is made with bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus, not Escherichia coli. The harmful Escherichia coli strains carrying numerous toxins are enterotoxigenic and enterohemorrhagic strains.
Enterotoxigenic and enterohemorrhagic strains

Correct. Escherichia coli is not always pathogenic, but its bad strains can carry numerous toxins; enterotoxigenic and enterohemorrhagic strains are the examples. The O157:H7 serotype is one of the worst culprits in outbreaks.
Spore-forming strains from soil and honey

Spores found in soil, on plants and in honey belong to the clostridia, Gram-positive rods; they are not a kind of Escherichia coli. The toxin-carrying Escherichia coli strains are enterotoxigenic and enterohemorrhagic strains.

mis.Fermenting strains used in yogurt making: beneficial fermenters confused with toxin strains

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Which bacteria are involved in turning milk into yogurt?
opts: Escherichia coli and Salmonella

These are foodborne pathogens: Escherichia coli is an indicator organism of fecal contamination, and Salmonella is associated mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles. Yogurt is made with Lactobacillus and Streptococcus.
Lactobacillus and Streptococcus

Correct. Yogurt is a type of fermented milk made with bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus. Cheese-making, by contrast, draws on yeast, bacteria and molds (multicellular fungi), and kefir, koumiss and buttermilk are other fermented milks.
Saccharomyces and Clostridium

Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast, a fungus) and certain Clostridium species are microbes of bread making, not of yogurt. Yogurt fermentation involves bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus.
Spirulina and other cyanobacteria
Spirulina is a cyanobacterium eaten directly as food, in smoothies and vitamin supplement gummies; it is not used to ferment milk. The bacteria involved in yogurt are Lactobacillus and Streptococcus.

mis.Spirulina and other cyanobacteria: microbe eaten as food confused with a fermenter

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: A person develops foodborne vibriosis. Which food most likely carried it?
opts: Peanut butter
Peanut butter has been a source of Salmonella, along with poultry, eggs, pet food and live backyard poultry. The foodborne route of Vibrio is seafood: shellfish, crabs, raw seafood and oysters.
Raw oysters

Correct. The foodborne route of vibriosis runs through seafood: shellfish, crabs, raw seafood and oysters. Vibrio species are salt-tolerant and live in ocean and estuarine waters, the source of those foods.
Soft cheese
Soft cheese is among the foods most vulnerable to Listeria monocytogenes, along with deli meats, hot dogs and smoked seafood. Foodborne vibriosis comes from shellfish, crabs, raw seafood and oysters.
Fried rice
Rice is often associated with the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning, which starts within 6 hours or less. Vibrio reaches people through seafood such as shellfish, crabs and raw oysters.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: In the food infection pathway, which step lets bacteria multiply in the food before it is eaten?
opts: Thorough cooking to 165 F

Cooking meat thoroughly, checked with a meat thermometer at 165 F rather than by guessing, is a preventive step, not the one that lets bacteria multiply. In the infection pathway, improper cooking technique is what allows the cells to grow in the food.
Toxin release into the food

Toxin release into the food is the intoxication pathway, in which the preformed toxin is ingested and reaches target organs. In food infection, live cells multiply in the food after improper cooking technique.
Ingestion of the cooked food
Ingestion comes after the bacteria have already multiplied; it delivers them to the intestine, where they cause infection. The step that lets them multiply in the food is improper cooking technique.
Improper cooking technique

Correct. In food infection, live cells in a food such as poultry come through improper cooking technique and multiply in the food; the larger number is then ingested and causes an intestinal infection. Salmonella and Listeria are the examples of this pattern.

mis.Thorough cooking to 165 F: preventive step mistaken for the hazard
mis.Toxin release into the food: intoxication step placed in the infection pathway

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Within a few hours of a summer picnic, several guests who ate fried rice develop vomiting and abdominal cramps. Which organism is the likely cause?
opts: Clostridium botulinum

Clostridium botulinum toxin causes paralysis of the muscles in the relaxed position and respiratory failure, not vomiting and cramps that pass. Rice, summertime and a rapid onset of vomiting point to Bacillus cereus.
Bacillus cereus

Correct. Bacillus cereus is a very common food poisoning agent, especially in summertime. Its emetic form is often associated with rice, and the intoxication has a rapid onset (6 hours or less) with vomiting and abdominal cramps that resolve on their own.
Campylobacter jejuni

Campylobacter jejuni causes rapid fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea, usually from raw poultry fluid or poultry leftovers. Vomiting and cramps within hours of eating rice point to the emetic form of Bacillus cereus.
Listeria monocytogenes

Listeria monocytogenes threatens pregnant women, unborn children, the elderly and immunocompromised people through soft cheeses, deli meats, hot dogs and raw produce. A rice dish with rapid vomiting and cramps fits Bacillus cereus.

mis.Listeria monocytogenes: adjacent foodborne bacterium (soft cheese, deli meats)

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Milk begins as a sterile mixture. How do microbes first get into it?
opts: On leaving the animal and from utensils

Correct. Milk begins as a sterile mixture of water, minerals, protein, butterfat, lactose and other sugars; microbes are introduced as it exits the female mammal's body and by milking utensils. Once contaminated it is highly susceptible to microbial growth because of its nutrient density.
They are already present in the udder

This contradicts the starting point: milk is a sterile mixture while still inside the animal. Microbes are introduced as it exits the female mammal's body and by milking utensils, and its nutrient density then lets them grow.
From yeast in human saliva

Saliva is the yeast source for some alcoholic beverages made from chewed plant material, not the route into fresh milk. Microbes enter milk as it exits the female mammal's body and from milking utensils.
When cheese molds are added to it

Molds, with yeast and bacteria, are used in cheese-making, an induced fermentation that comes later; adding them is not how microbes first reach fresh milk. That happens as milk exits the body and from milking utensils.

mis.They are already present in the udder: milk assumed contaminated inside the animal
mis.From yeast in human saliva: brewing yeast source borrowed into dairy
mis.When cheese molds are added to it: induced fermentation mistaken for the first contamination

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Which food-handling rule is given for preventing Bacillus cereus food poisoning?
opts: Preserve food in salt brine with vinegar

Salt brine, often with lactic acid, vinegar and spices, is used to pickle and preserve vegetables; it is a food-production method. The rule given for Bacillus cereus is to keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold.
Keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold

Correct. Bacillus cereus is a very common food poisoning agent, especially in summertime, and the rule given against it is to keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold. Its intoxication starts rapidly, within 6 hours or less, with vomiting and cramps.
Skip oysters in months without an R

The 'R-month' rule concerns oysters, clams and mussels and Vibrio, and it is now uncertain because aquaculture practices have advanced. For Bacillus cereus, the rule is to keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold.
Get a vaccine after a suspected exposure
A vaccine in case of suspected exposure belongs to the hepatitis viruses spread by the fecal-oral route. Bacillus cereus is prevented by holding temperatures: keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold.

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Escherichia coli is found everywhere, including inside healthy humans. What explains its presence without disease?
opts: It survives as dormant spores
Spore formation belongs to the clostridia, Gram-positive rods whose spores are found in soil, on plants and in honey. Escherichia coli lives in healthy people because not every strain is pathogenic.
Its illness takes weeks to appear

An incubation that can last from hours to weeks is a feature of salmonellosis, not the reason Escherichia coli lives in healthy people. The explanation is that not every strain is pathogenic, and the organism has good traits too.
It spoils food rather than infecting

Escherichia coli is described as an infectious agent and an indicator of fecal contamination, while spoilage of bread, cereals and acidic juices is tied to fungi. As an infectious agent it causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, but only its bad strains are harmful.
Not every strain is pathogenic

Correct. Escherichia coli is found everywhere, including inside humans, but it is not always pathogenic and has many good traits too. Illness comes from the bad strains, which can carry numerous toxins (for example enterotoxigenic or enterohemorrhagic strains).

mis.It spoils food rather than infecting: pathogen mistaken for a spoilage organism

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Which feature describes typhoid fever, the most severe enteric fever?
opts: Growth even at refrigerator temperatures

Growth from 1 to 40 C, including refrigerator temperatures, is the biggest concern with Listeria monocytogenes. Typhoid fever is instead marked by Salmonella typhi invading the intestinal wall and spreading to the blood and lymph nodes.
A tiny dose of a few particles
An infectious dose of only a few viral particles describes norovirus, not typhoid fever. Typhoid fever is marked by invasion of the intestinal wall, with spread to the blood and lymph nodes.
Invasion of the gut wall, then blood and nodes

Correct. Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is the most severe enteric fever, and it is marked by invasion of the intestinal wall, with possible spread to the blood and lymph nodes. Other forms of salmonellosis include gastroenteritis, septicemia, fever, shock and kidney dysfunction.
A preformed toxin that paralyzes muscles

A preformed toxin that paralyzes muscles describes botulinum toxin in food intoxication. Typhoid fever is an invasive Salmonella infection, marked by invasion of the intestinal wall and spread to the blood and lymph nodes.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: At what point does Clostridium botulinum start producing its toxin?
opts: When its spores germinate

Correct. When Clostridium botulinum spores germinate, they can start producing toxin, the botulinum toxin. The spores come from soil, plants or honey, and even if only a few bacteria are present they can produce plenty of the toxin.
When its cells form spores

Spore formation is the reverse step: spores are the form found in soil, on plants and in honey. Clostridium botulinum starts producing toxin when its spores germinate, and even a few bacteria can make plenty of it.
After live cells reach the gut

Live cells multiplying after they are eaten is food infection, as with Salmonella or Listeria. Botulinum toxin is made once the spores germinate, and botulism from food is an intoxication in which the toxin itself is ingested.
When it invades the gut wall

Invasion of the intestinal wall, with spread to the blood and lymph nodes, is typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi. Clostridium botulinum harms through a toxin that it starts producing when its spores germinate.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Foodborne Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora or Giardia typically causes which illness?
opts: Usually rapid bloody diarrhea with fever

Rapid fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea describe Campylobacter jejuni, a bacterium spread by raw poultry fluid. The foodborne protozoans cause milder diarrhea that usually resolves on its own.
Enteric fever spreading to the blood

Enteric fever with spread to the blood and lymph nodes is typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi, which invades the intestinal wall. Protozoans such as Giardia and Cyclospora cause mild, usually self-limiting diarrhea.
Paralysis of muscles in the relaxed position

Paralysis of muscles in the relaxed position, then respiratory failure, follows ingested botulinum toxin. Foodborne protozoans such as Cryptosporidium cause mild diarrhea that usually resolves without that danger.
Mild diarrhea that is usually self-limiting

Correct. The common foodborne protozoans, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia and Entamoeba, can all cause mild diarrhea that is usually self-limiting. It is associated with uncooked fruits and vegetables or drinking water.

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Why is Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary, remembered in food safety?
opts: She was the first person to die of typhoid

She is remembered as a source of infection, not as its first victim: despite warnings and an explanation, she persisted and caused multiple deadly outbreaks of typhoid fever, the most severe enteric fever.
She traced Salmonella to poultry and reptiles

Linking Salmonella mainly to poultry and aquatic reptiles is a reservoir fact, not her part in food safety. Typhoid Mary is remembered for persisting despite warnings and causing multiple deadly outbreaks.
She kept cooking despite warnings, causing outbreaks

Correct. Mary Mallon was warned and given an explanation, yet she persisted in preparing food and caused multiple deadly outbreaks. Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is the most severe enteric fever, so a single person handling food could spread it widely.
Her backyard hens spread Salmonella to others

Live poultry such as backyard hens is a Salmonella source, but that is not her story. Typhoid Mary was warned and given an explanation, yet persisted in preparing food and caused multiple deadly outbreaks.

mis.Her backyard hens spread Salmonella to o: animal source confused with a human source

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Which foodborne bacterium is a leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease each year in the United States?
opts: Listeria monocytogenes

Listeria monocytogenes is singled out as the number one cause of food-related deaths in the United States, not as a leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease. That description belongs to Campylobacter jejuni.
Clostridium botulinum

Clostridium botulinum causes botulism, in which ingested toxin paralyzes muscles in the relaxed position and can lead to respiratory failure; it is not a leading diarrheal cause. Campylobacter jejuni is.
Vibrio vulnificus

Vibrio vulnificus is a salt-tolerant species acquired from water (ingested or through wounds) or from shellfish and raw seafood; it is not the leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease. Campylobacter jejuni is.
Campylobacter jejuni

Correct. Campylobacter jejuni is a leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease each year in the United States, especially in children, and the illness is very much under-reported. Its infectious dose is under 500 bacterial cells.

mis.Listeria monocytogenes: leading cause of death confused with leading cause of diarrhea
mis.Clostridium botulinum: severe toxin illness confused with common diarrhea

set1.io: 4 — Correlate associations between improved laboratory analytical methods with respect to near-daily announcements of food recalls and food-related illness
set1.q: Which food safety responsibility rests with the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture rather than with local and state health departments?
opts: Conducting food safety surveillance

Surveillance is shared: local and state health departments, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other agencies are all tasked with it. What the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture add is enforcing food safety law and enacting policy.
Investigating illness outbreaks

Outbreak investigation is shared with local and state health departments and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. What sets the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture apart is law enforcement and policy enactment.
Hosting the PulseNet database

PulseNet, the database of pulsed-field gel electrophoresis patterns for microbial isolates, is run through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, not these two agencies. The Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture enforce food safety law and enact policy.
Enforcing food safety law and policy

Correct. Local and state health departments, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture all conduct surveillance and investigate outbreaks, but the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture are in charge of law enforcement and policy enactment.

mis.Conducting food safety surveillance: shared surveillance role taken as the distinguishing one
mis.Investigating illness outbreaks: shared investigative role taken as the distinguishing one
mis.Hosting the PulseNet database: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tool credited to the enforcing agencies

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Which set of foods is most vulnerable to Listeria monocytogenes?
opts: Eggs, peanut butter and pet food

Eggs, peanut butter and pet food are Salmonella sources, along with poultry products, live backyard poultry and sushi-grade seafood. The foods most vulnerable to Listeria monocytogenes include soft cheeses, deli meats and hot dogs.
Bread, cereals and acidic juices

Bread, cereals and acidic juices are foods that fungi spoil; fungi do not commonly cause disease. Listeria monocytogenes is a disease-causing bacterium, and its most vulnerable foods include soft cheeses, deli meats and hot dogs.
Soft cheeses, deli meats, hot dogs

Correct. The foods most vulnerable to Listeria monocytogenes are soft cheeses, raw fruit and vegetables, raw or undercooked meats, deli meats, seafood, smoked seafood, hot dogs and preserved meats. It also grows well at refrigerator temperatures, anywhere from 1 to 40 C.
Rice dishes kept warm on summer days

Rice, especially in summertime, is the setting for the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning, with rapid, self-resolving vomiting and cramps. Listeria monocytogenes targets soft cheeses, deli meats, hot dogs and smoked seafood.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: After a preformed toxin is swallowed in food intoxication, where does it act?
opts: The intestine, where it starts an infection

An intestinal infection is the end point of food infection, where live cells that multiplied in the food are ingested. A toxin swallowed in food intoxication is not an infection; it passes on to its target organs.
The liver and spleen, via the blood

Spread through the bloodstream to the liver, spleen, brain, placenta and fetus is the path of Listeria monocytogenes, a live-cell food infection. A preformed toxin acts on its target organs, such as the brain and muscles.
Lymph nodes, after invading the gut wall

Invasion of the intestinal wall with spread to the blood and lymph nodes describes typhoid fever, caused by live Salmonella typhi. A preformed toxin in food intoxication travels to target organs such as the brain and muscles.
Target organs such as brain and muscle

Correct. In food intoxication the ingested toxin passes through the gut to its target organs, such as the brain and the muscles. Botulinum toxin is an example: it paralyzes muscles in the relaxed position, which can lead to respiratory failure.

mis.The intestine, where it starts an infect: infection end point given for intoxication

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Which two Clostridium species are not food-related?
opts: Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium tetani
Clostridium tetani is not food-related, but Clostridium botulinum is a food species whose toxin causes foodborne botulism. The non-food pair is Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile.
Clostridium perfringens and Clostridium difficile
Clostridium difficile is not food-related, but Clostridium perfringens is listed with Clostridium botulinum among the food species. The non-food pair is Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile.
Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile

Correct. Of the notable clostridia, Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile are the two marked as not food-related. Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium perfringens are the food species, botulinum through the toxin behind foodborne botulism.
Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium perfringens

These are the two food-related species: botulinum toxin causes foodborne botulism, and perfringens is listed with it. The species set apart as not food-related are Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile.

mis.Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium pe: food species taken for non-food species

set1.io: 4 — Correlate associations between improved laboratory analytical methods with respect to near-daily announcements of food recalls and food-related illness
set1.q: Which agency runs PulseNet?
opts: Food and Drug Administration

The Food and Drug Administration posts updated information on food and dietary supplement recalls, including pet food, and enforces food safety law. PulseNet, the database of isolate patterns, runs through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
United States Department of Agriculture

The United States Department of Agriculture also has food recall information and shares law enforcement and policy duties with the Food and Drug Administration. PulseNet belongs to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Local and state health departments
Local and state health departments conduct food safety surveillance and outbreak investigations, but PulseNet, the pattern database, is run through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Correct. The pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern of each microbial isolate is added to PulseNet, a database run through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and reached from its website. It helps find outbreak causes and problems at food processing plants.

mis.Food and Drug Administration: recall agency confused with surveillance agency
mis.United States Department of Agriculture: recall agency confused with surveillance agency
mis.Local and state health departments: local surveillance confused with the national database

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Which group is named among those at greatest risk for both salmonellosis and listeriosis?
opts: Young children
Young children are at greatest risk for salmonellosis, but the listeriosis list names unborn children and premature babies rather than young children. The elderly are the group the two lists share.
Immunocompromised people
Immunocompromised people are among those at greatest risk for listeriosis, but the salmonellosis list names young children and the elderly. The elderly are the shared group.
Elderly people

Correct. Young children and the elderly are at greatest risk for salmonellosis. Pregnant women, unborn children, premature babies, elderly people and immunocompromised people are at greatest risk for listeriosis. The elderly are the group on both lists.
Pregnant women
Pregnant women are at greatest risk for listeriosis, but the groups at greatest risk for salmonellosis are young children and the elderly. The elderly, not pregnant women, appear on both lists.

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Leftover cooked chicken has sat in the refrigerator for an unknown time and smells normal. What should be done with it?
opts: Rinse it, then serve it cold

Washing is advised for fruits and vegetables, not as a fix for leftovers of unknown age. Listeria monocytogenes grows well at refrigerator temperatures, so the rule for doubtful food is to toss it out.
Toss it out rather than risk it

Correct. When in doubt, toss it out. Refrigeration does not settle the question: Listeria monocytogenes grows well at refrigerator temperatures, and with Campylobacter jejuni from poultry even one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness.
Eat it, since it still smells normal

A normal smell does not settle it: undesirable flavors, appearance or smell mark spoilage, which is separate from foodborne illness, and microbes can be present without changing the food. When in doubt, toss it out.
Taste a small bite first
Tasting is not a safe test: the infectious dose of Campylobacter jejuni is under 500 cells, so a tiny amount can cause illness, and poultry leftovers call for care. When in doubt, toss it out.

mis.Eat it, since it still smells normal: smell taken as a safety test
mis.Taste a small bite first: tasting taken as a safety test

set1.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set1.q: Why does norovirus spread so readily in daycares and nursing homes?
opts: A few viral particles can infect

Correct. The infectious dose of norovirus is only a few viral particles, and it spreads person to person through feces and vomitus. Together these drive outbreaks in daycares, nursing homes and cruise ships.
It grows well in chilled food

Growth from 1 to 40 C, including refrigerator temperatures, is the concern with Listeria monocytogenes. Norovirus spreads person to person through feces and vomitus, and its infectious dose is only a few viral particles.
Its spores survive in soil

Spores in soil, on plants and in honey belong to the clostridia. Norovirus spreads person to person through feces and vomitus in daycares and nursing homes, and only a few viral particles are needed to cause illness.
Its toxin forms before it is eaten

A toxin preformed in food is food intoxication, as with staphylococcal or botulinum toxin. Norovirus is a virus passed person to person through feces and vomitus, and only a few viral particles are needed to cause illness.

mis.Its toxin forms before it is eaten: intoxication confused with a viral infection

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Foodborne protozoan diarrhea is associated with which sources?
opts: Uncooked produce and drinking water

Correct. Protozoans such as Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia and Entamoeba cause mild diarrhea associated with uncooked fruits and vegetables or drinking water. Ready-to-eat salad bags are a common culprit of foodborne illness.
Undercooked pork and wild venison

Venison and pork carry tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis when the animal's muscle or organs were contaminated while it was alive. The protozoans are linked to uncooked fruits and vegetables and drinking water.
Raw shellfish from salty estuaries
Raw shellfish and other seafood from ocean and estuarine waters carry salt-tolerant Vibrio species. The foodborne protozoans travel instead in uncooked fruits and vegetables and in drinking water.
Raw honey and the soil around plants
Soil, plants and honey are where clostridial spores are found. Protozoans such as Giardia and Cyclospora cause mild diarrhea associated with uncooked fruits and vegetables or drinking water.

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Where are Vibrio species such as Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio vulnificus found?
opts: Poultry and aquatic reptiles

Salmonella is found mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles; the reptiles live in water, which makes this tempting. Vibrio species are the salt-tolerant bacteria of ocean and estuarine waters, carried by shellfish, crabs and raw seafood.
Ocean and estuarine waters

Correct. Vibrio species, including Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio vulnificus, are salt-tolerant bacteria found in ocean and estuarine waters. People acquire them from that water, swallowed or through wounds, or from seafood such as shellfish, crabs and oysters.
Birds, mammals and soil

Birds and mammals, with persistence in soil, describe Listeria monocytogenes. Vibrio species are salt-tolerant and live in ocean and estuarine waters, so their sources are seawater and seafood such as shellfish and oysters.
Soil, plants and honey

Soil, plants and honey are where clostridial spores are found. Vibrio species are salt-tolerant bacteria of ocean and estuarine waters, reaching people through water or through seafood such as shellfish and oysters.

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: In bread making, what do microbial enzymes acting on gluten give the dough?
opts: Elasticity that makes it workable

Correct. Conditioning is one of the three microbial functions in bread making: microbial enzymes act on gluten to give the dough elasticity, making it pliable and workable. Leavening (by gases) and flavor and aroma (by organic acids and alcohols) are the other two functions.
Rise from carbon dioxide gas

Rise is leavening, a separate function driven mainly by carbon dioxide and other gases, not by enzymes acting on gluten. The enzymes condition the dough instead, giving it elasticity so it is pliable and workable.
Flavor from organic acids

Flavor and aroma come from organic acids and alcohols, the second microbial function in bread making. Enzyme action on gluten is the third function, conditioning, which gives the dough its elasticity.
Preservation, as a salt brine does

Salt brine preserves vegetable material in pickling; preservation is not one of the bread-making functions. In bread, microbial enzymes acting on gluten condition the dough, giving it elasticity so it can be worked.

mis.Preservation, as a salt brine does: pickling fact borrowed into bread making

set1.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set1.q: Besides poultry meat, which routes carry Campylobacter jejuni to people in its transmission cycle?
opts: Contaminated water and milk from cattle

Correct. The Campylobacter jejuni transmission cycle reaches people by three routes: poultry meat, contaminated water, and milk from cattle. Poultry still needs particular care, since even one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness.
Vomitus and person-to-person contact

Spread person to person through feces and vomitus, as in daycares, nursing homes and cruise ships, describes norovirus. The Campylobacter jejuni cycle reaches people through poultry meat, water and milk from cattle.
Spores in soil and raw honey
Spores in soil, on plants and in honey belong to the clostridia. Campylobacter jejuni reaches people through poultry meat, contaminated water and milk from cattle.
Wounds exposed to seawater

Wound infection from water is a Vibrio route, from salt-tolerant species in ocean and estuarine waters. The Campylobacter jejuni cycle links chickens to people through poultry meat, water and milk from cattle.

set1.q: How does Listeria monocytogenes cause illness after a contaminated food is eaten?
opts: Live cells are ingested and multiply

Correct. Listeria is an example of food infection: live cells are ingested and multiply, often after improper cooking lets the bacteria multiply in the food, and the result is an intestinal infection. From the intestine it can spread through a lymph node and the bloodstream.
Its preformed toxin reaches target organs

A toxin already formed in the food that travels to target organs is food intoxication, as with staphylococcal toxin or Clostridium botulinum toxin. Listeria causes food infection: the live cells are eaten and multiply.
Its spores germinate and make toxin

Spores that germinate and start producing toxin describe Clostridium botulinum, whose spores are found in soil, on plants and in honey. Listeria monocytogenes causes illness as live cells that are eaten and multiply.
It spoils the food's flavor and smell

Spoilage makes food unfit through undesirable flavors, appearance or smell; it is a separate detrimental effect from foodborne illness. Listeria monocytogenes causes disease as a food infection, with live cells that multiply.

set2.q: Which set of complaints makes up the common symptoms of foodborne illness?
opts: Septicemia, shock and kidney dysfunction

These are among the severe forms salmonellosis can take, alongside gastroenteritis and enteric fever; they are not the common symptom set. Foodborne illness typically brings diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.
Infection of the placenta and fetus

Spread from the intestine through the bloodstream to the placenta and fetus is the specific pathway of Listeria monocytogenes, which is why pregnant women are at greatest risk from it. The common symptoms are diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.
Diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever

Correct. The symptoms of foodborne illness are diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever. Escherichia coli, for example, causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and Bacillus cereus intoxication causes self-resolving vomiting and abdominal cramps.
Muscle paralysis and respiratory failure

Paralysis of the muscles in the relaxed position, leading to respiratory failure, follows ingested botulinum toxin; it is a specific, severe outcome rather than the common picture. Foodborne illness typically brings diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.

set2.q: A chicken dish carrying Salmonella gives the diner gastroenteritis. Which kind of foodborne illness is this?
opts: A neutral microbial effect
A neutral effect means microbes are present but neither cause disease nor change the food; they are simply eaten with it. This diner became ill from live Salmonella, which makes it a food infection.
Food infection

Correct. Salmonella is a named example of food infection: live cells in a food such as poultry are ingested and cause an intestinal infection, with improper cooking technique letting them multiply in the food first. Gastroenteritis is one of the forms salmonellosis can take.
Food intoxication

Food intoxication is the ingestion of a toxin already formed in the food, as with staphylococcal or Clostridium botulinum toxin, which then acts on target organs. Salmonella is an example of the other kind: live cells that cause an intestinal infection.
Food spoilage
Spoilage renders food unfit to eat through undesirable flavors, appearance or smell; it is not an illness. Live Salmonella eaten in a chicken dish and causing gastroenteritis is food infection.

set2.q: Which of these fermented foods is a plant product rather than a fermented milk?
opts: Koumiss
Koumiss is a fermented milk product, grouped with kefir and buttermilk. Fermented plant products include soy sauce and tofu from soybeans, and vegetables pickled in salt brine.
Buttermilk
Buttermilk is a fermented milk product, as its name suggests, grouped with kefir and koumiss. Soy sauce, made by fermenting soybeans or their extracts, is the plant product here.
Soy sauce

Correct. Soybeans and their extracts are fermented to make tofu and soy sauce (shoyu), so soy sauce is a fermented plant product, like pickled vegetables. Kefir, koumiss and buttermilk are fermented milk products, grouped with yogurt.
Kefir

Kefir is a fermented milk product, named with koumiss and buttermilk as relatives of yogurt. The fermented plant product among these choices is soy sauce, made by fermenting soybeans or their extracts.

set2.q: How does ingested botulinum toxin lead to death?
opts: Rigid muscle spasm, then respiratory failure
This reverses the paralysis: botulinum toxin paralyzes muscles in the relaxed position, not in a rigid spasm. Respiratory failure and death follow from that relaxed paralysis.
Spread through the blood to the brain

Spread from the intestine through the bloodstream to the brain is the infection route of Listeria monocytogenes. Botulism is an intoxication: the toxin causes paralysis of muscles in the relaxed position, then respiratory failure.
Invasion of the gut wall and blood

Invasion of the intestinal wall, with spread to the blood and lymph nodes, is typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi. Botulinum toxin acts on muscles instead, paralyzing them in the relaxed position until breathing fails.
Relaxed paralysis, then respiratory failure

Correct. Ingesting botulinum toxin leads to paralysis of the muscles in the relaxed position, followed by respiratory failure and death. The toxin is made when spores germinate, and even a few Clostridium botulinum cells can produce plenty of it.

set2.q: Which description fits the clostridia?
opts: Gram-positive, non-spore-forming anaerobes
Clostridia do form spores, and those spores are found in soils, associated with plants and even in honey. The full description is Gram-positive rods that are strict anaerobes and form spores.
Gram-positive, spore-forming strict anaerobes

Correct. Clostridia are Gram-positive rods that are strict anaerobes and form spores. Their spores can be found in soils, associated with plants, or even in honey, and the food species are Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium perfringens.
Gram-negative, spore-forming strict anaerobes
The spore-forming and strict-anaerobe parts are right, but clostridia are Gram-positive rods, not Gram-negative. Their spores are found in soils, associated with plants and even in honey.
Gram-positive, spore-forming strict aerobes
Clostridia are strict anaerobes, the reverse of strict aerobes; the Gram-positive and spore-forming parts are right. They are Gram-positive rods whose spores turn up in soil, on plants and in honey.

set2.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set2.q: Why does keeping deli meats chilled fail to protect against Listeria monocytogenes?
opts: Its spores survive in the cold

Spores belong to the clostridia, which are spore-forming strict anaerobes found in soil, on plants and in honey. Listeria monocytogenes is a problem in chilled food because it keeps growing: it grows well from 1 to 40 C.
Its toxin forms before chilling

A toxin made in the food before it is eaten is food intoxication, as with staphylococcal or botulinum toxin. Listeria monocytogenes causes food infection, and its cells keep multiplying in chilled food because it grows well from 1 to 40 C.
Its infectious dose is under 500 cells

An infectious dose of fewer than 500 cells, so that one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness, is the Campylobacter jejuni figure, and it says nothing about cold. Listeria monocytogenes defeats chilling because it grows well from 1 to 40 C.
It grows well from 1 to 40 C

Correct. Probably the biggest concern with Listeria monocytogenes is that it grows well from 1 to 40 C, so it multiplies easily at refrigerator and room temperatures. Deli meats, soft cheeses, hot dogs and smoked seafood are among the foods most vulnerable to it.

set2.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set2.q: Which group of foods has been linked to Escherichia coli outbreaks?
opts: Ground beef, spinach and lettuce

Correct. Sporadic Escherichia coli outbreaks originate from fecally contaminated meats or vegetables: hamburgers and ground beef, bagged spinach and romaine lettuce are among the recorded sources, along with cookie dough and raw milk cheese.
Peanut butter, eggs and pet food

Peanut butter, eggs and pet food are sources of Salmonella, together with poultry products, live backyard poultry and sushi-grade seafood. Escherichia coli outbreaks have come from ground beef, spinach and romaine lettuce.
Fried rice and other rice dishes

Rice is often associated with the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning, which has a rapid onset of 6 hours or less. Escherichia coli outbreaks have come from fecally contaminated meats and vegetables such as ground beef and spinach.
Ice cream and smoked seafood

Ice cream recalls and smoked seafood point to Listeria monocytogenes, which grows well even at refrigerator temperatures. Escherichia coli outbreaks have come from ground beef, spinach and romaine lettuce.

set2.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set2.q: Which illness picture does Escherichia coli typically cause as an infectious agent?
opts: Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea

Correct. As an infectious agent, Escherichia coli causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, the familiar gastrointestinal picture of foodborne illness. Its bad strains can carry numerous toxins, and the O157:H7 serotype is one of the worst culprits.
Muscle paralysis and respiratory failure

Paralysis of muscles in the relaxed position, leading to respiratory failure, follows ingestion of Clostridium botulinum toxin. Escherichia coli as an infectious agent causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Enteric fever spreading to lymph nodes

Enteric fever with invasion of the intestinal wall and spread to the blood and lymph nodes is typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi. Escherichia coli as an infectious agent causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Infection of a seawater-exposed wound

Wound infection from water is one of the two routes of vibriosis, caused by salt-tolerant Vibrio species in ocean and estuarine waters. Escherichia coli as an infectious agent causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.

set2.q: The heading of this diagram has been removed. Which foodborne bacterium does it trace from contaminated food through the body?
opts: Salmonella typhi

Typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi does invade the intestinal wall and spread to the blood and lymph nodes, but its greatest-risk groups are young children and the elderly. The branch through the placenta to the fetus matches Listeria monocytogenes.
Campylobacter jejuni

The Campylobacter cycle runs from chickens, water, cattle and milk, and poultry meat to people, and its illness is rapid fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea. A path to the brain and through the placenta belongs to Listeria monocytogenes.
Clostridium botulinum

Botulism is a food intoxication: preformed toxin, not the bacterium itself, reaches the target organs and paralyzes muscles. A diagram of live bacteria moving through a lymph node, the blood, liver and spleen to the placenta is the infection route of Listeria monocytogenes.
Listeria monocytogenes

Correct. The path from contaminated food through the intestine, a lymph node and the bloodstream to the liver and spleen, then on to the brain and across the placenta to the fetus, is the spread of Listeria monocytogenes. It explains why pregnant women and unborn children are at greatest risk.

set2.q: Which measure helps prevent hepatitis A from spreading?
opts: Covering coughs and sneezes
Hepatitis A and E are not spread by sneezing; their route is fecal-oral. Prevention means good handwashing and diaper hygiene, cooking food thoroughly and consuming clean drinking water.
Handwashing and diaper hygiene

Correct. Hepatitis A and E spread by the fecal-oral route, so prevention means good handwashing and diaper hygiene, cooking food thoroughly and drinking clean water. They are not spread by kissing, sneezing, saliva or blood, and a vaccine exists for suspected exposure.
Avoiding kissing and shared drinks

Hepatitis A and E are not spread by kissing, sneezing, saliva or blood, so avoiding kissing does not address their route. Prevention means good handwashing and diaper hygiene, thorough cooking and clean water.
Screening donated blood
Hepatitis A and E are not spread by blood; they travel by the fecal-oral route. Good handwashing and diaper hygiene, thorough cooking and clean drinking water are what prevent them.

set2.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set2.q: Which ranking does Listeria monocytogenes hold among foodborne agents in the United States?
opts: Number one cause of food-related deaths

Correct. Listeria monocytogenes is the number one cause of food-related deaths in the United States. The groups at greatest risk for listeriosis are pregnant women, unborn children, premature babies, elderly people and immunocompromised people.
Leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease
Being a leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease in the United States, especially in children, is the ranking of Campylobacter jejuni. Listeria monocytogenes ranks first for food-related deaths.
Cause of the most severe enteric fever

The most severe enteric fever is typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, which invades the intestinal wall and spreads to the blood and lymph nodes. Listeria monocytogenes holds a different title: number one cause of food-related deaths.
Very common summertime food poisoner

Being a very common food poisoning agent, especially in summertime, describes Bacillus cereus, with its rapid, self-resolving vomiting and cramps. Listeria monocytogenes is singled out as the number one cause of food-related deaths in the United States.

set2.io: 2 — Correlate associations between contaminated foods with the increasing numbers of diagnosed food-borne illnesses and mortality worldwide
set2.q: How are tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis in meat best killed?
opts: A mild bleach rinse

Mild bleach cleaning solutions are for kitchen surfaces and utensils, not meat. Tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis are best killed by thorough cooking, since the meat may have been contaminated while the animal was alive.
Washing in hot, soapy water
Hot, soapy water is for handwashing. Worms in venison or pork can sit in the animal's muscle or organ meat, contaminated while it was alive, and they are best killed by thorough cooking.
A vaccine after exposure
A vaccine in case of suspected exposure is given for the fecal-oral hepatitis viruses. For tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis, the best protection is thorough cooking of the meat.
Thorough cooking

Correct. Tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis are best killed by thorough cooking. Venison, pork or other meats can be contaminated while the animal is still alive, so the muscle or organ meat itself may carry the worms.

set2.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set2.q: Which food is the diarrheal form of Bacillus cereus illness usually associated with?
opts: Meat

Correct. Bacillus cereus gastroenteritis is either diarrheal or emetic, and each form has its usual food: the diarrheal form is usually associated with meat, and the emetic form is often associated with rice.
Rice

Rice goes with the other form: the emetic form of Bacillus cereus illness is often associated with rice. The diarrheal form is usually associated with meat, so the food is the clue to which form a person has.
Honey
Honey is where clostridial spores can turn up, along with soil and plants. The diarrheal form of Bacillus cereus illness is usually associated with meat, and the emetic form with rice.
Oysters

Oysters, clams and mussels carry salt-tolerant Vibrio species from ocean and estuarine waters. The diarrheal form of Bacillus cereus illness is usually associated with meat, while the emetic form follows rice.

set2.io: 1 — Identify sources of microbial contamination in global food supply
set2.q: Which animals are the main reservoirs of Salmonella?
opts: Pigs and deer carrying worms

Pork and venison can be contaminated while the animal is still alive, but that concerns parasitic worms such as tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis. Salmonella is associated mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles.
Poultry and aquatic reptiles

Correct. Salmonella bacteria are associated with many animals, mainly poultry and aquatic reptiles. Matching sources include poultry products (chicken, turkey, duck), eggs and live poultry such as backyard hens.
Birds and mammals, persisting in soil

Birds and mammals, with persistence in soil, describe Listeria monocytogenes, the organism behind recalls of ice cream and cantaloupes. Salmonella is associated with many animals, but mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles.
Cattle that drink contaminated water
Cattle drinking contaminated water and passing the organism on in milk appear in the Campylobacter jejuni transmission cycle. Salmonella's main reservoirs are poultry and aquatic reptiles.

set2.q: How can shellfish come to carry norovirus?
opts: From spores in soil and on plants
Spores in soil, on plants and in honey are the clostridial form, and germinating spores make botulinum toxin. Norovirus reaches shellfish through water contaminated with feces.
By natural growth in salty seawater
Salt-tolerant growth in ocean and estuarine waters describes Vibrio species, a bacterial hazard of shellfish. Norovirus is a virus that reaches shellfish through water contaminated with feces.
From infected animals while alive
Contamination while the animal is still alive is the route of tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis in venison and pork. Norovirus gets into shellfish through feces-contaminated water.
From feces-contaminated water

Correct. Norovirus spreads mainly person to person through feces and vomitus, but it can also be spread by contaminated shellfish, which come from feces-contaminated water. Good handwashing, thorough cooking and clean drinking water are part of prevention.

set2.q: Which presentation is among the forms salmonellosis can take?
opts: Hepatitis from the fecal-oral route

Hepatitis A and E viruses are the ones typically spread by the fecal-oral route; hepatitis is not among the forms of salmonellosis, which include gastroenteritis, enteric fever, septicemia and kidney dysfunction.
Spread across the placenta

Spread through the bloodstream to the placenta and fetus is the Listeria monocytogenes pathway, which is why pregnant women are most at risk from it. Salmonellosis forms include gastroenteritis, enteric fever, septicemia and kidney dysfunction.
Septicemia, a blood infection

Correct. Salmonellosis can appear as gastroenteritis, enteric fever, septicemia (blood infection), fever, shock and kidney dysfunction. Its most severe enteric fever is typhoid fever, in which the bacteria invade the intestinal wall and spread to the blood and lymph nodes.
Paralysis of relaxed muscles

Paralysis of the muscles in the relaxed position, leading to respiratory failure, is caused by ingested botulinum toxin, not by Salmonella. Salmonellosis appears as gastroenteritis, enteric fever, septicemia, fever, shock or kidney dysfunction.

opts: Salmonella

Salmonella is associated mainly with poultry and aquatic reptiles and is traced through foods such as eggs, peanut butter and poultry products. The organism eosin methylene blue plates are used to confirm in food and water is Escherichia coli.
Listeria monocytogenes

Listeria monocytogenes is found in birds and mammals, persists in soil and grows from 1 to 40 C; it is not the organism these plates confirm. Eosin methylene blue plates are used to confirm Escherichia coli in food and water samples.
Campylobacter jejuni

Campylobacter jejuni is tied to raw poultry and its leftovers and has an infectious dose under 500 cells; it is not what these plates confirm. Eosin methylene blue plates confirm Escherichia coli in food and water samples.

set2.q: After cutting raw chicken, a cook rinses the knife in cold water and then slices salad vegetables on the same cutting board. Which kitchen rule does this break?
opts: Avoid cross-contamination of utensils

Correct. Raw chicken fluid left on the board and knife can reach the salad, which is cross-contamination of cutting boards and utensils. With Campylobacter jejuni the infectious dose is under 500 cells, so even one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness.
Keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold

Holding temperatures matter for Bacillus cereus, but nothing here was left warm or cool too long. The fault is moving raw poultry fluid onto the salad through a shared board and knife, which is cross-contamination.
Use a meat thermometer rather than guessing
A meat thermometer checks that meat reaches 165 F, but the chicken's cooking is not the problem described. Using the same board and knife for raw chicken and salad is cross-contamination.
When in doubt, toss it out

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

set2.q: An illness cluster is traced to eggs from one farm and to a batch of peanut butter. Which organism do these sources point to?

Correct. Eggs and peanut butter are both Salmonella sources, along with poultry products, pet food, live backyard poultry and sushi-grade seafood, and Salmonella recalls have included peanuts and peanut butter and farm eggs.
Escherichia coli O157:H7

Listeria monocytogenes

Bacillus cereus

set2.q: What must happen for a food infection, as opposed to a food intoxication, to occur?
opts: A toxin must be formed before eating
A toxin formed in the food before it is eaten defines food intoxication, as with staphylococcal or botulinum toxin. Food infection instead requires live bacterial cells to be ingested.
The toxin must reach target organs

Spores must germinate in the soil

Live bacterial cells must be ingested

set2.q: Which statement describes the place of fungi in food safety?
opts: Rarely disease, but production and spoilage

Correct. Fungi do not commonly cause disease, but they are associated with both food production and food spoilage: mushrooms as food, yeasts for fermenting many products, penicillin in medicine, and spoilage of bread, cereals and acidic juices.
The most common foodborne pathogens

Bacteria, not fungi, are the most common foodborne pathogens. Fungi do not commonly cause disease; they matter in food production (mushrooms, yeasts for fermenting) and in spoilage of bread, cereals and acidic juices.
Parasites best killed by thorough cooking

Thorough cooking is the best way to kill tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis, the parasitic worms. Fungi do not commonly cause disease; they are associated with food production and with spoilage of bread, cereals and acidic juices.
Agents of mild diarrhea from drinking water

Mild, usually self-limiting diarrhea from drinking water or uncooked produce is caused by protozoans such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium. Fungi do not commonly cause disease; they matter in food production and spoilage.

set2.q: How does the acceptance of microbial additives differ between animal feed and human food?
opts: Still being researched for both

Research (for example on single cell protein) describes the human side; microbial additives for animal feed are already used. The two differ: feed has taken them up, while human versions are slower to be accepted.
Used in feed; slower to be accepted for people

Correct. Microbial additives for animal feed are already used, but human versions are slower to be accepted. Single cell protein and other bacterial or fungal products are still being researched, although the cyanobacterium Spirulina is already added to some foods in the United States.
Used in human food; slower for animal feed

This reverses the pattern. Microbial additives are already used in animal feed; it is the human versions that are slower to be accepted, with single cell protein and similar products still being researched.
Accepted equally in both feed and food

Acceptance is not equal. Additives for animal feed are already in use, while human versions lag behind and are slower to be accepted, although Spirulina is already added to smoothies and vitamin supplement gummies.

mis.Still being researched for both: research stage applied to feed as well

set2.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of Campylobacter jejuni illness?
opts: Self-resolving vomiting and cramps
Rapid, self-resolving vomiting and abdominal cramps within 6 hours describe Bacillus cereus intoxication. Campylobacter jejuni instead brings fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea.
Spread to the placenta and fetus

Spread through the bloodstream to the placenta and fetus is the Listeria monocytogenes pathway, which puts pregnant women at greatest risk. Campylobacter jejuni causes fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea.
Muscle paralysis and respiratory failure

Paralysis of muscles in the relaxed position with respiratory failure follows ingested botulinum toxin. Campylobacter jejuni illness is marked instead by fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea.
Fever, headache, dizziness, bloody diarrhea

Correct. Campylobacter jejuni illness brings fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea, usually rapid in onset. Even one drop of raw poultry fluid can be enough, since the infectious dose is under 500 cells.

set2.q: How do the two forms of Bacillus cereus gastroenteritis differ in the heat stability of their toxins?
opts: Both forms from heat-stable toxins

The two forms do not share one toxin type: the diarrheal form comes from a heat-stable toxin and the emetic form from a heat-labile toxin. That difference, with meat for the diarrheal form and rice for the emetic form, separates them.
Both forms from heat-labile toxins
A heat-labile toxin is given for the emetic, rice-associated form only; the diarrheal, meat-associated form is attributed to a heat-stable toxin. The two forms differ in their toxins.
Diarrheal heat-stable; emetic heat-labile

Correct. The diarrheal form of Bacillus cereus illness is attributed to a heat-stable toxin, usually with meat, and the emetic form to a heat-labile toxin, often with rice. Many references give the reverse pairing; the pairing keyed here is diarrheal heat-stable, emetic heat-labile.
Diarrheal heat-labile; emetic heat-stable

This is the reverse of the pairing keyed here, which puts the heat-stable toxin with the diarrheal, meat-associated form and the heat-labile toxin with the emetic, rice-associated form. Many references do describe it this way round, so know that the two versions exist.

set2.q: These band patterns come from bacterial isolates in one outbreak: an earlier patient for comparison, five patients, five environmental samples and three animals. Which laboratory method produced them?
opts: Gram staining of each isolate

Gram staining shows cell traits such as the Gram-positive rods of the clostridia; it gives no band pattern for each isolate. Rows of bands matched across patients, environment and animals come from pulsed-field gel electrophoresis.
Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis

Correct. A pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern is made for each microbial isolate and added to PulseNet. Here the patient, environmental and animal isolates share one band pattern while the earlier comparison patient differs, the kind of match that helps find an outbreak's cause.
Eosin methylene blue plate culture

Eosin methylene blue plates are used to confirm Escherichia coli in samples such as food and water; the result is colonies on a plate, not a row of bands for each isolate. Band patterns matched across isolates come from pulsed-field gel electrophoresis.
A PulseNet database search

PulseNet is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention database the patterns are added to, not the method that makes them. Each isolate's band pattern is produced by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis and then entered into PulseNet.

set2.q: When cooking meat products, what temperature should a meat thermometer confirm instead of guessing?
opts: 110 F falls well short of the 165 F a meat thermometer should confirm. Improper cooking lets bacteria multiply in the food, the start of a food infection such as salmonellosis or listeriosis.
130 F is still below the 165 F target for cooked meat products. Raw or undercooked meats are among the foods most vulnerable to Listeria monocytogenes, which is why the thermometer replaces guessing.

Correct. When cooking meat products, the advice is to use a meat thermometer and confirm 165 F rather than guessing. Proper cooking matters because improper cooking lets bacteria in the food multiply, the route of food infection.
190 F overshoots the figure given: the meat thermometer target for cooked meat products is 165 F. The point is to measure rather than guess, so the meat reliably reaches 165 F.

set2.q: Which food calls for particular care to prevent Campylobacter jejuni illness?
opts: Peanut butter and peanuts
Peanut butter is a Salmonella source, with recalls of peanuts and peanut butter; it is not linked to Campylobacter jejuni, whose concern is poultry, including holiday birds and their leftovers.
Cooked rice and rice dishes
Rice is often associated with the emetic form of Bacillus cereus, a rapid-onset intoxication. Campylobacter jejuni is tied to poultry instead: a single drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness.
Poultry, including its leftovers

Correct. Campylobacter jejuni comes with poultry: even one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness, and holiday poultry and its leftovers deserve particular care. In its transmission cycle, chickens and poultry meat lead to people.
Bagged ready-to-eat salads

Ready-to-eat salad bags are a common culprit of foodborne illness, named with the protozoa (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia) that come with uncooked produce. The particular care for Campylobacter jejuni is with raw poultry and its leftovers.

set2.q: What are the two major routes of vibriosis?
opts: Soil spores and wound contamination

Spores in soil and wound-borne illness belong to the clostridia, whose spores also turn up on plants and in honey. Vibrio lives in ocean and estuarine waters; its routes are water (ingested or via wounds) and seafood.
Infected live animals and pet feces

Meat contaminated while the animal was still alive and domestic pet feces are the sources of tapeworm and roundworm. Vibrio is a salt-tolerant bacterium of ocean and estuarine waters, acquired from water or seafood.
Water (ingested or wounds) and seafood

Correct. Two major routes of vibriosis are known: water, either ingested or through wound infections, and food, such as shellfish, crabs, raw seafood and oysters. Both trace back to the salt-tolerant Vibrio species of ocean and estuarine waters.
Person-to-person contact and raw shellfish

Person-to-person spread through feces and vomitus, plus contaminated shellfish, is the pattern of norovirus. Vibrio's two routes are water, ingested or through wounds, and food such as shellfish, crabs and raw oysters.
